references.text: Parallel passage in the Sermon on the Mount where Jesus uses the same illustration of a father giving good gifts to his children: 'Is there anyone among you who, if your son asks for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a snake?' This is the closest parallel to Luke 11:11.

The immediate context that continues the illustration: If earthly fathers know how to give good gifts to their children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him.
Context in Matthew's parallel: 'Ask and it will be given to you; seek and you will find; knock and the door will be opened to you.' Same context as Luke 11:9-10, which immediately precedes the verse.
The closest context in Luke leading up to the illustration of the father and son: 'Ask and it will be given to you; seek and you will find; knock and the door will be opened to you.'

'For the Lord God is a sun and shield. The Lord bestows favor and honor; no good thing does He withhold from those who walk in integrity.' This psalm emphasizes that God does not hold back good gifts from His children, the same theme as Jesus' illustration.

'Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights.' James emphasizes that God gives good gifts, which aligns with Jesus' point that a father does not give something harmful instead of something good.
'He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all, will He not also graciously give us all things with Him?' Paul uses a similar 'how much more' argument about God's generosity.
'Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb?' God compares His care to a parent's natural love, the same type of argument Jesus uses here.
